title: Momoweta
summary: Momoweta was a Corchaug sachem associated with the North Fork during the mid-seventeenth century.
content:
Momoweta was a Corchaug sachem associated with the North Fork in the mid-seventeenth century. Colonial records document his diplomacy in 1644 and his appearance in a 1648 North Fork deed, but the cited sources do not establish his birth or death dates.

His name appears in several variant spellings, including Moughmaitow, Mamaweto, Mamawichtouw, Mamawetough, Mowmetow, and Momowetow.2

Historical Context

In 1644, the Plymouth colonial record places Momoweta, written Moughmaitow, before the Commissioners of the United Colonies seeking peace and protection.2

On May 6, 1648, he appears in the North Fork deed context involving Corchaug territory, Paucuckatux, Mattituck/Cutchogue, and Plum Island.12

These records preserve important evidence of Corchaug diplomacy and land pressure, but they were written in colonial legal settings rather than in Momoweta's own voice.1

References

  1. John A. Strong, The Algonquian Peoples of Long Island from Earliest Times to 1700.
  2. William Wallace Tooker, Indian Place-Names on Long Island and Islands Adjacent, pp. 181-182.
  3. Records of the Colony of New Plymouth in New England, vol. IX, p. 18.
why_this_matters: Momoweta shows Corchaug leadership as active and diplomatic in the colonial record, while also revealing how much of Native leadership survives only through documents written by colonial authorities.
